questions.answer: One query loads a list, then one more query runs for each item to load its related data (e.g. lazy loading in a loop)
distractors: A query that returns one more row than expected
Running N queries in parallel, plus one to combine their results
An index with one more column than the query needs
questions.explanation: Fifty orders become 51 round trips. Load the related data in the same query with Include, or project just what you need with Select.

questions.prompt: Which EF Core method loads related entities as part of the same query, e.g. orders together with their customer?
questions.explanation: `context.Orders.Include(o => o.Customer)` is eager loading. `Entry(x).Reference(...).Load()` is explicit loading, a separate query later.

questions.prompt: Which method do you add to a read-only EF Core query so the context doesn't track the entities it returns?
questions.explanation: Tracking keeps a snapshot of every entity for change detection. For data you won't save, AsNoTracking is faster and uses less memory.

questions.prompt: Which DI lifetime does `AddDbContext` register the DbContext with?
questions.explanation: One DbContext per request: it's a short-lived unit of work and not thread-safe, so it must not be a singleton.

questions.prompt: Can two threads safely use the same DbContext instance at the same time?
distractors: Yes, as long as they only read
questions.explanation: Even reads mutate the change tracker. EF Core throws when it detects a second operation starting on the same context; give each concurrent operation its own context (IDbContextFactory).

questions.prompt: Why is `context.Users.AsEnumerable().Where(u => u.Age > 30)` much slower than `context.Users.Where(u => u.Age > 30)` on a big table?
questions.answer: AsEnumerable switches to LINQ to Objects, so every user is loaded and filtered in memory instead of in SQL
distractors: AsEnumerable caches the whole table, so it's actually faster after the first call
It isn't: both translate to the same SQL
AsEnumerable runs a separate query for each user
questions.explanation: Operators after AsEnumerable bind to Enumerable, not Queryable, so EF Core can't see them. The SQL becomes SELECT * FROM Users and the WHERE happens in your process.

questions.prompt: Which interface does `context.Users.Where(...)` return, carrying an expression tree that EF Core translates into SQL?
questions.explanation: Queryable.Where takes an Expression<Func<T, bool>>, data describing the lambda, which the provider turns into SQL. Enumerable.Where takes a compiled Func and runs it in memory.

questions.prompt: By default, how does `SaveChanges()` run all the pending inserts, updates and deletes?
questions.answer: Together in a single transaction: all succeed or none do
distractors: Each statement in its own transaction
Only the first change; call it again for the rest
questions.explanation: If no transaction is already open, SaveChanges starts one around the whole batch and rolls it back on failure. You only need an explicit transaction to span several SaveChanges calls.

questions.prompt: Which `dotnet ef` command creates a new migration from your model changes?
questions.explanation: `migrations add` generates the migration code; `database update` applies pending migrations to the database; `migrations script` produces SQL to run elsewhere.

questions.prompt: Which exception does EF Core's `SaveChanges()` throw when an optimistic concurrency check fails because the row changed since it was read?
questions.explanation: With a concurrency token ([Timestamp]/rowversion or [ConcurrencyCheck]), the UPDATE includes the original value in its WHERE clause; zero rows affected means someone else changed it. OptimisticConcurrencyException is the old EF6 name.

questions.prompt: Which EF Core query method loads each included collection with its own SQL query, avoiding the duplicated rows ("cartesian explosion") of one big JOIN?
questions.explanation: Including two collections in one query multiplies rows (orders × lines × payments). Split queries fetch each collection separately; the trade-off is more round trips and no single consistent snapshot without a transaction.

questions.prompt: Which method shows the SQL that an EF Core LINQ query will run, without executing it?
questions.explanation: `query.ToQueryString()` returns the generated SQL (with parameter declarations). For every query the app runs, turn on logging with LogTo or the Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Database.Command category.
